title: panic/recover and an error strategy across layers
summary: Errors are for failures a correct program expects; panics are for bugs. Recover only at boundaries you own, the top of a goroutine and the top of a request, and let every other layer return errors upward.

examples.title: Errors for input, panics for bugs, and what recover hands you

annotations.note: Must functions panic by convention (regexp.MustCompile, template.Must). Use them only on inputs fixed in the source: a typo then fails the first test run or program start, never a request.
recover returns any, so a type switch sorts it. A runtime.Error is a failure the runtime detected, such as a nil map write or an index out of range: always a bug, never a condition to handle.

One mistake, two APIs. Compile returns an error because its input may come from a user; MustCompile panics because its input is code. Its panic value is a plain string, so it lands in the default case.
Nothing at this level can handle these sensibly. The right response is a 500 at the boundary, a log entry with the stack, and a fix.
Before Go 1.21, panic(nil) made recover return nil, so a boundary checking r != nil let the panic vanish. Now it raises *runtime.PanicNilError; GODEBUG=panicnil=1 restores the old behavior.

examples.title: Recover at the top of each goroutine and report a typed error

annotations.note: A distinct type lets callers tell bugs from failures with errors.AsType. A failure can be retried or shown to the user; a bug needs its stack logged and someone told.

The deferred recover must run in the goroutine that panics. A recover in main, or in the function that started the goroutine, never sees this panic, and an unrecovered panic in any goroutine ends the whole process.
debug.Stack() still includes the panicking line here, because the deferred function runs on top of the panicking frames. Once it returns they are gone, so capture the stack now, not later.
sync.WaitGroup.Go (Go 1.25) bundles Add, go and Done, and its documentation says f must not panic: hence safely. Each goroutine writes only its own slot, and Wait makes the writes visible.
Three outcomes: success, an ordinary failure, and a bug. Without safely, job 2 would have crashed the program and taken the other results with it.

examples.title: One place for status codes, logging and recovery in an HTTP server

annotations.note: Handlers return an error, as in the Go blog's appHandler pattern. They don't write error responses themselves; ServeHTTP does, once, for every route.
The request boundary. http.ErrAbortHandler means "abort this response quietly", so it is re-panicked for net/http to handle; swallowing it would turn a deliberate abort into a logged 500.
The single place errors become status codes. errors.Is finds ErrNotFound however deeply it was wrapped. Unexpected errors are logged here, once, and the client gets a 500 without internals.
Without a boundary of your own, net/http recovers the panic, logs a stack trace to the server's error log (see stderr), and closes the connection. The client gets no status code at all.

/raw: a dropped connection. /users/7: a mapped 404, not logged, because it isn't a server problem. /users/0: a recovered 500. stderr shows both logs; it is never compared, which is just as well, since it holds a port number and timestamps.

use_cases: Must helpers for constants: regexp.MustCompile, template.Must, parsing embedded config at startup
Panicking on a violated invariant: the default branch of a switch over your own enum, an impossible state in a state machine
Recovering at the top of worker goroutines, consumers and scheduled jobs so one bad item doesn't stop the process
Recovery middleware in HTTP and gRPC servers that logs the stack and answers 500
strengths: Expected failures stay ordinary values, so control flow is visible in the code, unlike exceptions that can come out of any call
A panic is loud: it carries a stack trace and, unrecovered, stops the process instead of leaving it running in a corrupted state
Boundaries are explicit: you can point at the two or three places in a codebase where recover is allowed
weaknesses: An unrecovered panic in any goroutine kills the whole process, unlike Java or Python, where an uncaught exception ends only its thread
Each goroutine needs its own recover boundary and nothing adds one for you: even sync.WaitGroup.Go only documents that f must not panic
recover works only when called directly by a deferred function, a rule that is easy to break with a helper

pitfalls.title: Expecting main's recover to catch a goroutine's panic
pitfalls.detail: recover only sees panics in its own goroutine. Put the deferred recover inside the function the goroutine runs.

pitfalls.title: Calling a recover helper from a deferred closure
pitfalls.detail: defer logPanic() works when logPanic calls recover. defer func() { logPanic() }() does not: recover is then called by logPanic, not directly by the deferred function, and returns nil.

pitfalls.title: Recovering deep inside the code
pitfalls.detail: A recover in the middle of a call chain hides the bug and leaves state half-updated: a mutex held, a transaction open, a slice half-written. Recover at boundaries, fail that unit of work, log the stack.

pitfalls.title: Panicking for expected failures in a library
pitfalls.detail: Callers can only handle it with recover. "Not found", invalid input and timeouts are errors; the Code Review Comments say: don't use panic for normal error handling.

pitfalls.title: Swallowing http.ErrAbortHandler
pitfalls.detail: httputil.ReverseProxy and others panic with it to abort a response. A recovery middleware should re-panic it, not log a 500.

quiz.q: A goroutine started by main panics. main has defer func() { recover() }(). What happens?
quiz.why: recover only stops a panic in its own goroutine; an unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the program.

quiz.q: Which situation calls for a panic rather than an error?
options: A user submits an invalid email
A switch over your own enum reaches a value that can't exist
quiz.why: Only the impossible enum value is a bug in the program; the rest are failures a correct program must expect.

quiz.q: An HTTP handler panics and no middleware recovers it. What does the client get?
options: No response: the connection is closed
quiz.why: net/http recovers per request, logs the stack and closes the connection (or resets the HTTP/2 stream); it sends no status.

quiz.q: Where should HTTP status codes be chosen?
options: In one place at the HTTP boundary, from errors.Is and errors.AsType
quiz.why: Lower layers return domain errors; one boundary maps them to status codes, so the mapping stays consistent and the layers stay independent of HTTP.

further_reading.title: The Go Blog: Defer, Panic, and Recover
The Go Blog: Error handling and Go (the appHandler pattern)
The Go Programming Language Specification: Handling panics
package net/http: Handler (panic behavior) and ErrAbortHandler
Go Code Review Comments: Don't Panic

body:
## Concept

Go has two failure channels. Errors carry failures a correct program must expect: bad
input, a missing row, a timeout, an upstream returning 503. Panics signal bugs: a nil map
write, an index out of range, a broken invariant, a constant regular expression that
doesn't compile. A panic unwinds its goroutine, running deferred calls on the way; if
nothing recovers it, the program prints the panic value and a stack trace and exits with
status 2.

`recover` belongs at boundaries you own, where one unit of work may fail without taking
the rest down: the top of each goroutine you start, and the top of each request. There
the panic becomes a logged bug report plus an ordinary error or a 500. Everywhere else,
let it propagate. The defer lesson showed the mechanics of `recover`; this lesson is
about where it goes.

Errors travel the other way. Each layer returns them upward with context, translates
the ones that cross a package boundary, and exactly one place, the HTTP boundary or
`main`, decides what the outside world sees and logs the failure once.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/Python: a panic is like an unchecked exception that nobody is meant to catch, and
  `recover` is the catch at the thread or request boundary. The difference that bites:
  an uncaught exception in a Java or Python thread ends only that thread, while an
  unrecovered panic in any goroutine ends the whole process.
- Node: closer to Go. An uncaught exception crashes the process, and so does an unhandled
  promise rejection by default since Node 15.
- React: an error boundary is the UI-side version of the HTTP recover boundary: it stops
  one broken subtree from blanking the whole page (lesson ts.errors.result).
- C++: an unrecovered panic is like `std::terminate` after an uncaught exception, except
  that Go runs the panicking goroutine's deferred calls first.

## How it works

```text
layer            returns                               decides
repository       domain errors with context            driver errors -> ErrEmailTaken (%w) + text (%v)
service          domain errors with more context       business rules; knows nothing about HTTP
HTTP boundary    status code and body                  errors.Is/AsType -> 4xx/5xx; logs 5xx once;
                                                       recover -> log stack, 500
goroutine top    an error in a channel or slot         recover -> *PanicError with the stack
main             exit code                             logs once; os.Exit(1) after cleanup
```

Only the last three rows contain `recover` or `log`. A request handler that starts its
own goroutines needs a goroutine boundary inside them as well: the HTTP boundary only
covers the handler's own goroutine.

## Design notes

Panic for programmer errors only: violated invariants, unreachable branches of your own
switches, and `Must` calls on constants. Library code should never panic on bad input,
because its callers can only handle that with `recover`. At each boundary, log the panic
value together with `debug.Stack()` from inside the deferred function, since the
panicking frames are gone once that function returns. Fail that unit of work and keep
the process running. A recovered handler can only send a 500 if it hasn't written the
response headers yet; after that, logging and closing is all that's left. Keep
`log.Fatal` and `os.Exit` in `main`, after cleanup, as the defer lesson explained. And
map errors to status codes in one place, so a new domain error needs one new case, not a
hunt through every handler.

expected.bugs-vs-errors:
slug ok: true
error: error parsing regexp: missing closing ]: `[a-z`
string: regexp: Compile(`[a-z`): error parsing regexp: missing closing ]: `[a-z`
runtime.Error: assignment to entry in nil map
runtime.Error: runtime error: index out of range [3] with length 3
runtime.Error: runtime error: panic called with nil argument
no panic
expected.goroutine-boundary:
job 0: <nil>
job 1: upstream returned 503
job 2: bug: assignment to entry in nil map (stack captured: true)
process still running
expected.http-boundary:
/raw      no response: net/http recovered and dropped the connection
/users/7  404 not found
/users/0  500 internal error
